replies.author: @GeographyEffect
replies.text: Cheap Columbia Basin power does help explain why so many data centers ended up in central Washington, but it’s not the only reason why Amazon and Microsoft themselves are based around Seattle. Microsoft moved there long before the data-center era, and Amazon chose the region for factors including its tech talent base. But cheap power helps!

comments.author: @discovertheworld365
comments.text: The fascinating part is how geography quietly shapes economic power. Rivers aren’t just water routes. They determine where cities emerge, industries concentrate, and trade becomes possible. The Mississippi’s influence is a perfect reminder that America’s economic map was largely written by nature long before modern infrastructure.

comments.author: @BiffWellendorf
comments.text: Check out Rock Island Dam. It was  the first dam on a the Columbia River.

replies.author: @GeographyEffect
replies.text: That's an interesting piece of the river's early dam history. Rock Island was the first dam to span the Columbia, completed in 1933, just before the larger federal dam-building era really took off.

comments.author: @johntex105
comments.text: The Columbia is a vital river for the Northwestern US.  The Hydropower it has and does provide are crucial for that part of the country.   However to say it powers America is a gross overstatement.  Less than 6 percent of US electricity production is from Hydo.  Yes, Hydo power contributed to the development of nuclear weapons and energy at Hanford.   You could say the same about Oak Ridge or Los Alamos.  All that aside, the most important US river is the Mississippi, and it's not even close.

replies.author: @GeographyEffect
replies.text: Definitely agree that the Mississippi is more important for navigation and trade, while the Columbia is unusually important for hydropower because of its combination of volume and vertical drop.
